title: The Gibeonites (Joshua 9)
hookLine: tricked into a treaty, Israel keeps its oath anyway

cards: Dry bread, gone moldy and crumbling. Wineskins split and tied back together. Sandals patched and worn through.
Clothes worn old. A group of strangers walks into Israel's camp at Gilgal carrying all of it like evidence. We've come from a very far country, they say.
Look at our bread: it was warm from the oven the day we left. Make a treaty with us. They are lying.
They live just over the hills, in Gibeon, and they've heard what happened at Jericho and Ai. The costume is the whole plan.

teach.b: And it works. The men of Israel look at the bread, taste it, and take it as proof. The text stops to point out what they skip: they didn't ask counsel of the Lord.
Joshua makes peace with them, and the leaders of the congregation swear an oath to let them live. A few days later the truth comes out. The far country is next door.
The people are furious, and grumble against their leaders.

teach.h: WE HAVE SWORN: WE MAY NOT TOUCH THEM.
teach.b: And the leaders say the sentence the chapter turns on: we have sworn to them by the Lord, the God of Israel, so we may not touch them. The oath was gotten by a lie. It still holds.
The Gibeonites are spared, and they become, in the text's phrase, "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the people and for the altar. Did the oath bind as a valid contract?
Some rabbis in the Talmud say no: it was made under false pretenses, but breaking it would have disgraced God's name before the nations. Either way, the promise outlives everyone in the room.
Much later, the book of Samuel tells of a famine in King David's day, and traces it back to Saul, who had attacked the Gibeonites though Israel had sworn to them. The oath at Gilgal still bound.
A psalm describes the person who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and one line fits this chapter exactly: "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not."

how: In Jewish law vows and oaths are binding; the Kol Nidrei service on the eve of Yom Kippur addresses vows, and some Jews say bli neder, "without a vow", when promising something, to avoid an unintended oath.

o: a far-off people who came seeking a trade route
Jericho's allies who fought Joshua at Ai
neighbors who tricked Israel into a binding oath

games.q: the treaty at Gilgal — tap the pairs.

s: Israel's leaders asked God before making the treaty
they took the visitors' bread as proof and didn't ask counsel of the Lord. the text points it out.
when the trick came out, the leaders kept the oath
we have sworn to them by the Lord, so we may not touch them.
the oath was forgotten after Joshua's day
the book of Samuel traces a famine in David's day back to Saul breaking it.

games.q: you're one of Israel's leaders. days after swearing peace, you learn the far-off strangers live next door. the people are angry. what do you do?
o: cancel the treaty: it was made by a lie.
keep the oath, and give them work for the community.
drive them away without harming them.
games.why: the leaders keep the oath: we have sworn, we may not touch them. the Gibeonites become hewers of wood and drawers of water.

practice: Bring to mind one promise that has become inconvenient: made too fast, or the situation changed, or, like Israel's leaders, you'd have said no if you'd known more.
Don't decide yet whether you're bound; just picture keeping it, the actual hour, the actual phone call, and notice what it costs and what it would say about your word.
If you pray, hold the psalm's line: he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.

wordCard.voice: The Gibeonites. The neighbors who tricked Israel into a treaty, and were protected by the oath anyway. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: an oath. the leaders spare Gibeon because of the oath they swore.
